notes.title: V1.5.0 — The Production Hardening Update
notes.description: V1.2 gave the platform a project management brain. V1.5 gave it a spine transplant, a UX facelift, and an admin control panel that actually controls things. We fixed 45 API endpoints, aligned the database schema with reality, rebuilt the Admin Roles page from the ground up, and made the entire UI consistently green-and-white because brand consistency is not optional. The platform didn't just get stable — it got production-ready. No more 500 errors on page load. No more phantom columns. No more infinite loops. Just software that works.

notes.title: 45 API Endpoints Fixed: The Great 500 Purge
notes.description: We systematically tested every critical API endpoint and fixed every single one that returned a 500. Active sessions had an integer cast issue — fixed. Operational exceptions referenced columns that didn't exist — fixed. Procurement routes tried to join on a non-existent linked_invoice_capture_id — removed. The counterparties summary crashed when entity_assignments didn't exist — created the table and added a graceful fallback. The quality dashboard failed because qc_item_evidence was missing a project_id column — added it. If your endpoint was broken, it isn't anymore. If it was working, we didn't touch it. That's the rule.

notes.title: Schema Alignment: The Database Now Matches the Code
notes.description: We discovered that the Drizzle ORM schema and the actual PostgreSQL database had diverged like two old friends who stopped returning each other's calls. Six tables were missing columns. Two tables didn't exist at all. We created counterparty_contacts, entity_assignments (with proper enums), added is_active to users and counterparties, added role_tags and updated_at to counterparties, added project_id to qc_item_evidence, and added authority_model to role_permissions. Every migration is idempotent with IF NOT EXISTS guards and lives in the startup orchestrator. The schema and the database are speaking again.

notes.title: Admin Roles & Permissions: Now Actually Functional
notes.description: The Roles & Permissions page was rebuilt with a side-by-side layout — role list fixed on the left, permission detail panel on the right. No more scrolling past fourteen role cards to find the permissions section. The Navigation tab now uses the correct section keys matching the actual database, so toggling sections actually works. The Authority Model tab shows all entities with switches and scope dropdowns for every role, not just the ones with pre-existing entity permissions. The permission matrix, overview, navigation, authority model, users, and effective access tabs all work. You can now actually control who sees what, which is supposedly the entire point of a permissions system.

notes.title: Light Theme Consistency: Green Means Go, White Means Clean
notes.description: The entire application now uses a consistent white-and-emerald (#16A34A) theme. KPI cards use white backgrounds with emerald borders and icons — no more coloured gradient fills that looked like a PowerPoint from 2008. The due-this-week quick filter badges were changed from violet to emerald-600. Source filter active states use emerald-600. The Authority Model info banner changed from violet to emerald. Every card, every badge, every button — one palette, one brand, zero confusion.

notes.title: My Tasks Infinite Loop: The Bug That Loved Itself Too Much
notes.description: The My Tasks page had a useEffect that created a new object reference every render, which triggered a state update, which triggered a re-render, which created a new object reference, which — you get the idea. Maximum update depth exceeded. We replaced the useEffect plus setState synchronisation pattern with a useMemo that produces a stable reference. The unified detail task is now computed once per dependency change, not infinity times per frame. React is calm. The browser is calm. Everyone is calm.

notes.title: Navigation Cleanup: Less Chrome, More Content
notes.description: The breadcrumb bar now only renders when it actually has breadcrumbs or secondary nav items. Previously it rendered an empty 48px chrome bar on every page, burning vertical space for no reason. The Home sub-nav was renamed from 'Dashboard' to 'Home' because that's what it is. A leftover 'Actions Active' mobile floating badge from a previous experiment was removed — it was technically functional but aesthetically abandoned, like a gym membership in February.

notes.title: Homepage Redesign: Role-Specific Content That Knows Who You Are
notes.description: The home page now shows role-specific content based on your actual role. COO gets operational oversight. CFO gets financial summaries. Project Managers get their active projects. Engineers get their task queues. Company priorities display for everyone because alignment is not role-specific. The quick-link grid resolves to valid routes that actually exist. The dashboard loads real data from real endpoints that return real responses. Revolutionary, we know.

notes.title: Startup Orchestrator: One Place for All Migrations
notes.description: All additive database migrations now live in server/bootstrap/startup-orchestrator.ts. Every migration uses IF NOT EXISTS guards for idempotency. Tables, columns, enums — everything gets aligned on boot. No more drizzle-kit push. No more hoping the schema matches. The orchestrator runs once on startup, logs what it did, and moves on. If you add a column to the Drizzle schema, you add a migration to the orchestrator. One rule, one place, zero surprises.

notes.title: Easter Egg Status Update
notes.description: Still undiscovered. The easter egg has now survived a complete production hardening pass, a UI theme overhaul, a navigation restructure, and a permissions rebuild. It watched 45 endpoints get fixed and didn't need fixing itself. It has started to suspect it might be the most stable feature in the application. The irony is not lost on it. It has considered filing a bug report about the fact that nobody has found it, but decided that would be too meta even for software.
